title: How Infants Tune In to Speech — Werker & Tees's 6-to-12-Month Head-Turn Narrowing, Maye's Bimodal vs. Unimodal Distributions, Kuhl's Live-vs.-Video Mandarin & Lytle's Peer Contingency

teenKit.tldr: Babies start life as universal linguistic superheroes able to hear every sound in every human language, but they morph into native-language specialists by ruthlessly pruning away the distinctions they don't hear around them.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how your brain hardwires itself to your native tongue reveals that sometimes becoming an expert requires giving up raw, unfiltered potential.
keyTakeaways: At six months old, infants are 'universal listeners' who can effortlessly distinguish phonetic contrasts across every language on earth, from Hindi retroflexes to English stops.
Perceptual narrowing isn't a failure or a loss of intelligence, but a necessary neurological trade-off where the brain specializes in the native language by deleting unused pathways.
Social connection and statistics matter immensely: babies don't just passively absorb sounds, but use statistical frequencies in their environment and live social interaction to master language.

vocab.meaning: An infant who can hear and differentiate every subtle phonetic sound made across all human languages.
The smallest unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word, like the 'b' in bat versus the 'p' in pat.
The developmental process where the brain trims away its ability to detect sensory contrasts it isn't regularly exposed to.
A pattern in data showing two distinct peaks of frequency, which helps infant brains realize two different sounds exist.

quiz.question: What happens to a baby's phonetic perception between 6 and 12 months of age?
options: They magically learn to speak three new languages fluently.
They undergo perceptual narrowing, losing the ability to distinguish non-native speech sounds.
They become permanently unable to learn any new languages.
Their brain stops growing new neurons entirely.
quiz.explanation: Babies transition from universal listeners to native specialists by pruning away the ability to hear foreign phonetic contrasts.

quiz.question: According to Maye's research, how do infants figure out where phonetic boundaries lie in a new language?
options: By tracking the statistical distribution of sounds they hear around them.
By reading facial expressions and body language.
By mimicking adult mouth shapes automatically.
Through genetic coding that is pre-programmed at birth.
quiz.explanation: Infants track statistical patterns, like bimodal distributions, to automatically calculate where one speech sound ends and another begins.

quiz.question: Why did Patricia Kuhl's experiments show that babies learning Mandarin from a live speaker succeeded while those watching a video failed?
options: The video quality was too blurry for babies to see mouth movements.
Infants require social interaction and human contingency to truly unlock language acquisition.
Babies are naturally afraid of screens.
Recorded audio lacks high-frequency sound waves.
quiz.explanation: Language learning is fundamentally a social experience that relies on real-time human connection and contingency rather than passive media consumption.
